groups.high: An mRNA COVID-19 vaccine supplies temporary genetic instructions for producing the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, rather than a live virus. Lipid nanoparticles protect the messenger RNA and facilitate cellular uptake and release into the cytoplasm. Ribosomes translate its sequence into protein. The mRNA does not need to enter the nucleus or alter DNA, and cellular processes subsequently degrade it. Antigen presentation activates adaptive immunity: B cells produce antibodies, while T cells help coordinate responses or recognize infected cells. Memory B and T cells support later responses, although protection against infection is neither absolute nor permanent. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman's 2005 work demonstrated that modified nucleosides could reduce unwanted innate inflammatory recognition of synthetic RNA. Later research improved protein production and delivery. This was not a discovery that methylating cytidine disables a DNA receptor. The specific nucleoside chemistry differs between formulations. Nanoparticle composition, RNA design, dose, and storage influence performance. Neither a universal 30–60-minute in-body half-life nor guaranteed sterilizing immunity follows from the platform. Its practical advantage is that a known antigen sequence can be used to design and manufacture an adaptable vaccine, subject to safety and effectiveness testing.
groups.mid: An mRNA COVID-19 vaccine gives cells short-term instructions to make the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. It does not give you a live virus, and tiny fat-based packages, called lipid nanoparticles, protect the messenger RNA, or mRNA. They help it enter cells and reach the cytoplasm, the space outside the cell's nucleus, where ribosomes are the cell's protein-making tools. They read the instructions and build the protein. The mRNA does not need to enter the nucleus or change DNA. The cell later breaks it down. Your immune system learns from the protein. B cells make antibodies, while T cells help manage the response or find infected cells. Some B and T cells remain as memory cells. They help the body respond later, but cannot promise complete or lasting protection from infection. In 2005, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman showed that changes to RNA building blocks could reduce unwanted inflammation. Later work improved protein production and delivery. They did not simply change cytidine to switch off a DNA sensor. The exact changes vary by vaccine. RNA design, dose, storage, and the fat package all matter. There is no single 30–60-minute lifetime for vaccine RNA in the body. A strength of this approach is that scientists can use a known protein sequence to design a vaccine. It still needs safety and effectiveness tests.
groups.low: An mRNA COVID-19 vaccine gives your cells a short set of instructions. These tell cells to make the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, a part of the virus, not a live virus. Small fat-based packages, called lipid nanoparticles, protect the instructions. The instructions are messenger RNA, or mRNA. They reach the cytoplasm, the space outside the cell's nucleus. Ribosomes, the tools cells use to make proteins, read them. The mRNA does not have to enter the nucleus and does not change your DNA. Your cells later break it down. Your body's defence system learns to spot the spike protein. B cells make antibodies to help fight the virus. T cells help lead the response or find infected cells. Some B and T cells stay as memory cells to help if the virus comes back. This does not mean you can never get infected. Protection can fade. In 2005, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman found a way to change RNA building blocks. This reduced unwanted swelling and other immune alarm signals. Later work made delivery and protein production better. They did not just change cytidine to turn off a DNA sensor. The RNA changes vary by vaccine. Dose, storage, RNA design, and the fat package matter too. There is no fixed 30–60-minute life for vaccine RNA in your body. Scientists can use a known protein sequence to design a new vaccine. They must still test how safe it is and how well it works.
groups.source_review: Checked Nobel scientific account and CDC mechanism summaries. No patient-specific vaccine advice or universal pharmacokinetic claim.
groups.notes: Corrected erroneous cytidine/OAS/PKR/TLR9 account, paper venue implication, guaranteed sterilizing protection, and unsupported half-life; preserved mechanism, immune memory, delivery, and platform implications.

groups.high: CRISPR-Cas9 is an RNA-guided DNA-cutting system adapted from bacterial immunity. Jinek and colleagues' 2012 study showed that Cas9 could use a CRISPR RNA and a trans-activating CRISPR RNA, or an engineered single-guide RNA combining their functions, to cleave a chosen DNA sequence in vitro. The guide is an RNA molecule associated with Cas9, not a protein fused to the enzyme. For Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9, targeting generally requires a nearby NGG protospacer adjacent motif, or PAM, as well as sufficient guide–DNA complementarity. Cas9's HNH domain cuts the guide-complementary strand; its RuvC domain cuts the other strand. Together they produce a double-strand break. In cells, non-homologous end joining can repair that break with insertions or deletions. Some disrupt a coding sequence and knock out gene function, but not every repair creates a knockout. Alternative repair pathways can support more precise changes under suitable conditions. Nickases, inactive Cas9, and base editors are distinct engineered approaches, not requirements of the original experiment. The breakthrough was programmable DNA cleavage; it did not establish unrestricted targeting, perfect specificity, or successful editing of every organism. Off-target cutting, delivery, and variable repair outcomes require evaluation.
groups.mid: CRISPR-Cas9 is a tool for cutting DNA at a chosen site. It comes from a defence system in bacteria, and in 2012, Jinek and colleagues showed how to guide the Cas9 enzyme with two RNA parts. They also joined the parts into one single-guide RNA. The test cut DNA outside living cells. The guide sticks to Cas9 and matches a stretch of DNA; it is not a protein fused to the enzyme. A short nearby DNA sign, called a PAM, must also be present. For Cas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes, that sign is usually NGG. Cas9 has two cutting parts. HNH cuts the strand that matches the guide, while RuvC cuts the other strand. This makes a break across both strands, which a cell then tries to repair. One repair route, non-homologous end joining, can add or lose small bits of DNA. This may switch off a gene, but some repairs leave it working. Other repair routes can allow more precise changes in suitable conditions. Nickases, inactive Cas9, and base editors are other forms of the tool, but the original test did not need them. The key finding was that changing the RNA guide could change the DNA target, not that every target was reachable or every cut was right. Delivery, cuts at wrong sites, and the result of repair must all be checked.
groups.low: CRISPR-Cas9 is a tool that can cut DNA at a chosen spot. It comes from a way bacteria defend themselves, with Cas9 as the part that cuts. RNA is the part that guides it, and in 2012, Jinek and colleagues used two RNA parts to guide Cas9. They also made one single-guide RNA from those parts and cut DNA in a lab test, outside living cells. The guide joins Cas9, but it is not a protein stuck onto Cas9. The guide must match the DNA at the target. A small DNA sign, called a PAM, must be nearby too. For Cas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes, it is often NGG. Cas9 has two cutting parts, with HNH cutting the DNA strand matched by the guide. RuvC cuts the other strand, so the cut breaks both strands. A cell tries to fix the break through ways such as non-homologous end joining. It can add or lose small DNA bits, which may turn a gene off but do not always do so. Other kinds of repair can make more exact changes when the conditions are right. Nickases, inactive Cas9, and base editors are other forms of the tool, not needed for this first test. The guide can be changed to choose a new target, but not all targets work. Scientists must check delivery, cuts in the wrong place, and how the cell fixes each cut.
groups.source_review: Read primary study abstract and publisher summary. Distinguished 2012 in-vitro findings from later cellular repair applications.
groups.notes: Corrected false protein-guide fusion, nickase requirement, unlimited targeting, and automatic knockout.

groups.high: Quantum computers encode information in qubits rather than only classical bits. A qubit can have a superposition described by amplitudes for 0 and 1; their squared magnitudes determine measurement probabilities and sum to one. An n-qubit state has 2 to the power n basis components, but measurement does not expose all those components as readable answers. For 50 qubits the number is approximately 1.13 quadrillion, not a quintillion. Quantum gates transform amplitudes. Carefully designed interference can suppress unwanted outcomes and increase the likelihood of useful ones. Entanglement creates correlations that cannot be reproduced by independent qubit descriptions; it does not transmit information faster than light. Algorithms such as Shor's factoring algorithm and Grover's search algorithm offer particular theoretical advantages, not universal acceleration. Quantum simulation is another important application. General optimization speedups are problem-dependent, and classical computers also use parallel processing. Noise, decoherence, imperfect gates, and the substantial overhead of error correction constrain practical computation. Some hardware requires dilution refrigerators, while other platforms have different environmental requirements. Quantum computing therefore complements classical computing rather than replacing it with an engine that solves every difficult problem.
groups.mid: A normal computer uses bits with values of 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses qubits. A qubit can be in a superposition: a mix of the states 0 and 1. Numbers called amplitudes describe that mix. Squaring their sizes gives the chances of each result, which add up to one. With n qubits, the state has 2 to the power n basic parts. For 50 qubits that is about 1.13 quadrillion parts, not a quintillion. But reading the qubits does not give every possible answer. Quantum gates change the amplitudes. A well-designed algorithm uses interference to cancel some unwanted results and make useful ones more likely. Entanglement links qubits in ways that separate descriptions cannot capture. It cannot send messages faster than light. Shor's algorithm can help with factoring numbers. Grover's algorithm can speed up a type of search. Simulating molecules and other quantum systems is another use. These gains apply to certain problems, not all tasks. Faster optimization is not guaranteed. Normal computers can also do work in parallel. Noise and errors can spoil the fragile quantum state. Correcting errors uses many extra resources. Some machines need very cold fridges; not every design does. Quantum computers are tools to work alongside normal computers, not a way to solve every hard problem.
groups.low: A normal computer uses bits. A bit has a value of 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses qubits. A qubit can have a mix of the states 0 and 1. This mix is called superposition. Numbers called amplitudes describe it. Their squared sizes give the chance of each result. Those chances add up to one. With n qubits, there are 2 to the power n basic parts in the state. With 50, that is about 1.13 quadrillion. It is not a quintillion. This does not mean you can read out all the answers. Quantum gates change the mix. A plan, or algorithm, can make some results cancel out. It can make useful results more likely. This is called interference. Entanglement is a special link between qubits. It does not let you send messages faster than light. Shor's algorithm helps factor numbers. Grover's algorithm speeds up a kind of search. These machines may also model molecules and other quantum systems. They do not speed up every task. A gain in optimization is not assured. Normal computers can work on tasks in parallel too. Noise and small errors can spoil a quantum state. Fixing errors needs many extra resources. Some machines need very cold fridges. Others use different designs. Quantum and normal computers can work together. Neither tool solves every hard problem.
groups.source_review: Checked IBM's qubit and foundations material; independently checked 2^50 arithmetic.
groups.notes: Corrected parallel-readout myth, 50-qubit numerical mistake, faster-than-light implication, deterministic measurement, universal speedup, and universal cooling claims.

groups.high: Deuterium–tritium fusion combines two hydrogen isotopes to form helium-4 and a neutron, releasing approximately 17.6 MeV: 3.5 MeV in the helium nucleus and 14.1 MeV in the neutron. Deuterium has one proton and one neutron; tritium has one proton and two neutrons. A sufficiently hot, dense, well-confined plasma permits fusion despite electrostatic repulsion. ITER targets temperatures around 150 million degrees Celsius, rather than treating 100 million as a precise universal threshold. Magnetic fields confine charged particles in its tokamak. Helium nuclei heat the plasma, while uncharged neutrons escape magnetic confinement and transfer energy to surrounding structures. Future power plants would also need tritium breeding and heat-to-electricity systems. ITER, in France, is an experimental installation, not an electricity-generating plant. Its target plasma gain Q is at least 10: 500 MW of fusion power for 50 MW of external plasma heating. Q excludes many facility energy requirements, so Q=10 does not mean tenfold electrical output or guaranteed commercial viability. Q=1 is plasma heating breakeven, not ignition. Materials durability, fuel supply, heat removal, and reliable operation remain essential engineering challenges.
groups.mid: Fusion joins small atomic nuclei to release energy. ITER plans to join deuterium and tritium, two forms of hydrogen. Deuterium has one proton and one neutron. Tritium has one proton and two neutrons. They form helium-4 and a free neutron. The reaction releases about 17.6 MeV of energy: 3.5 MeV in helium and 14.1 MeV in the neutron. The fuel must be very hot, dense enough, and held long enough, which helps the nuclei get past their electric repulsion. ITER aims for about 150 million degrees Celsius. There is no single exact 100-million-degree threshold for all fusion. Its tokamak uses magnetic fields to hold charged particles. The helium helps keep the fuel hot. Neutrons have no charge, so they escape those fields and heat nearby structures. A future power plant would need ways to make more tritium and turn heat into electricity. ITER is an experiment in France that will not sell electricity. Its target is Q of at least 10: 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of heating put into the plasma. Q does not count all the power used by the site. It does not prove a profitable power plant. Q=1 means plasma heating breakeven, not a fully self-heated reaction. Strong materials, fuel supplies, cooling, and reliable running are still needed.
groups.low: Fusion joins the centres of small atoms. It gives off energy, and ITER will use deuterium and tritium. Both are forms of hydrogen; deuterium has one proton and one neutron. Tritium has one proton and two neutrons. When they join, they make helium-4 and a free neutron. They give off about 17.6 MeV of energy. The helium gets 3.5 MeV, while the neutron gets 14.1 MeV. The fuel must be very hot, dense enough, and held for long enough. This helps the atom centres get close, though their electric charges push them apart. ITER aims for about 150 million degrees Celsius. Not all fusion has a fixed threshold of 100 million degrees. The hot fuel is called plasma, and a ring-shaped machine, a tokamak, holds charged particles with magnets. Helium helps heat the plasma. The neutron has no charge, so it leaves the magnetic trap and heats nearby parts. A future power plant must make more tritium and turn heat into electricity. ITER is a test site in France and will not sell electricity. Its goal is Q of at least 10, which means 500 MW of fusion heat from 50 MW of plasma heating. Q leaves out other power used by the site, so it does not mean ten times as much electricity. Q=1 means heat in equals fusion heat out. It is not full self-heating. Fuel, strong materials, cooling, and reliable use are still hard problems.
groups.source_review: Checked ITER's temperature, energy-gain definition, thermal output target, and experimental purpose.
groups.notes: Corrected temperature, breakeven/ignition conflation, electricity implication, and claim that Q=10 alone ensures commercial feasibility.

groups.high: Neuralink's described N1 implant is an intracortical brain–computer interface with 1,024 recording electrodes distributed across 64 flexible threads. A surgical robot places threads in brain tissue associated with movement intention. The implant records electrical activity, processes signals, and transmits neural data wirelessly to software on an external device. Decoding software learns associations between recorded activity and intended actions, allowing a participant to control a computer cursor or other supported interface without ordinary limb movement. Recording sites are not equivalent to 1,024 independently identified neurons, and this is not unrestricted reading of thoughts. Calibration and adaptation are necessary because neural signals and the interface can change over time. The public PRIME study description does not establish a particular CNN or RNN architecture, a mandatory sub-10-millisecond latency, a grid of electrodes, or a universal ability to distinguish arbitrary limb movements. Surgical risks, infection, tissue response, thread movement, and loss of usable signals require monitoring. Flexible threads are intended to reduce mechanical mismatch but cannot guarantee the absence of scarring. Clinical findings must be interpreted within the tested devices, participants, tasks, and follow-up period; demonstrated cursor control does not establish a cure for paralysis.
groups.mid: Neuralink's N1 implant links brain signals to a computer. This is a brain–computer interface, or BCI. Its described design has 1,024 recording electrodes on 64 thin, flexible threads. A surgical robot places the threads in brain areas linked to plans for movement. The implant records electrical activity. It processes the signals and sends data without wires to software on a nearby device. The software learns which patterns go with actions the person intends. This can let a participant move a cursor without moving a hand. Each electrode is not a separate named neuron. The device cannot read every thought. It also needs training and adjustment, since brain signals can change. The public PRIME study description does not prove that it uses a specific CNN or RNN learning model. Nor does it promise a delay below 10 milliseconds, a fixed electrode grid, or control of any movement you choose. Surgery, infection, the body's response, thread movement, and lost signals are risks to track. Flexible threads may reduce strain between the device and brain tissue. They cannot promise no scars. Results apply to the people, devices, tasks, and follow-up time actually studied. Moving a cursor is a useful step, but it is not a cure for paralysis.
groups.low: Neuralink's N1 implant can link brain signals to a computer. This is called a brain–computer interface, or BCI, with 1,024 recording points called electrodes. These sit on 64 thin, soft threads. A robot helps place the threads in brain areas used to plan movement. The implant picks up electrical signals. It processes them and sends data without wires to software on a nearby device. The software learns which signal patterns go with the moves a person plans. A participant may then move a cursor without moving a hand. One electrode does not mean one known brain cell. The device does not read all thoughts. It needs practice and checks because brain signals can change, so the setup may need to change too. The public PRIME study does not prove which CNN or RNN model the software uses. It does not promise a delay of less than 10 milliseconds. It does not prove that the points form a grid or can read every planned move. Surgery and infection are risks, and the body may react to the implant. Threads may move, and signals may be lost. Soft threads may put less strain on tissue, but they cannot stop all scarring. Results show what the tested people did with the tested device. The tasks and time studied matter. Cursor control may help, but it is not a cure for paralysis.
groups.source_review: Checked manufacturer PRIME study descriptions; treated as design and study claims, not independent proof of clinical effectiveness.
groups.notes: Removed invented electrode layout, neuron mapping, decoder architecture, mandatory latency, and deterministic motor-intent claims.

groups.high: Amine-based post-combustion carbon capture generally uses chemical absorption into a liquid solvent, not adsorption onto a solid. Flue gas contacts an aqueous amine, such as monoethanolamine, in an absorber. Carbon dioxide reacts reversibly with the solvent; depending on the amine and conditions, carbamate or bicarbonate species form. The carbon-rich solvent passes to a regeneration unit, where heat releases a concentrated carbon dioxide stream. Lean solvent returns to the absorber, while the separated gas is conditioned, compressed, and transported for suitable use or geological storage. Systems can capture 90% or more of the carbon dioxide in their treated gas, but capture performance depends on design, gas composition, solvent flow, and operating conditions. This is not automatically a 90% reduction in total lifecycle emissions. Solvent regeneration consumes substantial energy. Heat recovery and improved solvents can reduce this burden. Water management, impurities, corrosion, solvent degradation, and amine emissions also require control. Capture percentage differs from product purity. Further treatment depends on transport and storage specifications; cryogenic distillation is not universally necessary. Flue-gas carbon dioxide partial pressure must be assessed for the particular source, not assumed to exceed atmospheric pressure. Permanent climate benefit also requires verified, durable storage and accounting for added energy use.
groups.mid: Amine carbon capture takes carbon dioxide, or CO2, out of waste gas. It usually uses a liquid, not a solid surface. This is absorption, not adsorption. Waste gas passes through a tower with water and an amine, such as monoethanolamine. CO2 reacts with the liquid. It can form carbamate or bicarbonate, based on the type of amine and the conditions. The CO2-rich liquid then goes to a second unit. Heat frees the gas. The liquid can go back and catch more. The freed CO2 is cleaned, compressed, and sent for a suitable use or storage deep in rock. A system can catch 90% or more of the CO2 in the gas it treats. The result depends on its design, the waste gas, liquid flow, and how it runs. This does not mean it cuts all emissions over its whole life by 90%. Heating the liquid takes energy. Better liquids and reused heat can cut that cost. Plants must also manage water, dirt in the gas, rust, worn-out solvent, and amine releases. The share of CO2 caught is not the same as the purity of the final gas. Extra cleaning depends on how the gas will be moved and stored. Deep cooling is not always needed. CO2 pressure varies with the source. A climate benefit needs safe long-term storage and a count of the extra energy used.
groups.low: Amine carbon capture takes CO2 out of waste gas. CO2 is carbon dioxide, and the process usually uses a liquid. The gas goes into the liquid, not just onto a solid surface, which is called absorption. The waste gas flows through a tower with water and an amine, such as monoethanolamine. CO2 joins with the amine. The products may be carbamate or bicarbonate. The type of amine and the way the plant runs affect this. The CO2-rich liquid goes to a unit that heats it. Heat frees the CO2, and the liquid goes back to catch more gas. The CO2 is cleaned and squeezed to take up less space. It can then be moved for a suitable use or stored deep in rock. A plant can catch 90% or more of the CO2 in the gas it treats. Its design, gas mix, liquid flow, and use all matter. This does not mean all its emissions fall by 90%. Heating the liquid uses energy, but better liquids and reused heat can help. Workers must manage water, dirt, rust, worn-out liquid, and amine leaks. How much CO2 is caught is not the same as how pure it is. Extra cleaning depends on where it goes next. Deep cooling is not always needed. CO2 pressure differs by source. To help the climate, storage must last and the extra energy used must be counted too.
groups.source_review: Checked DOE/NETL solvent technology, capture targets, and regeneration requirements.
groups.notes: Corrected adsorption/absorption, implausible CO2 partial pressure, capture/purity conflation, and universal purification assumptions; restored corrupted explanation.

groups.high: Graphene is a single atomic layer of carbon arranged in a hexagonal honeycomb lattice. Strong in-plane carbon bonds give a nearly defect-free sheet exceptional tensile properties. Laboratory measurements report intrinsic strength around 130 GPa and a Young's modulus around 1 TPa. Describing it as about 200 times stronger than steel is an approximate comparison that depends on the steel grade and test; it is not a guarantee for every graphene product. Strength measures resistance to breaking, whereas stiffness measures resistance to stretching. Delocalized electrons support unusual electrical transport, often described using a zero-gap electronic structure and Dirac-like dispersion. High carrier mobility and thermal conductivity depend on sample quality, temperature, substrate, and measurement method, so headline values are not universal specifications. Defects, grain boundaries, wrinkles, and contamination can diminish performance. Exfoliation separates layers from graphite; chemical vapor deposition grows films on suitable surfaces. Producing large, consistent, transferable sheets remains an engineering challenge. Sliding between layers concerns multilayer materials, not the intrinsic failure of an isolated monolayer. Applications therefore require testing the manufactured material, not merely citing ideal single-sheet properties.
groups.mid: Graphene is a sheet of carbon just one atom thick, and its atoms form a six-sided pattern, like a honeycomb, and strong bonds within the sheet make good samples hard to break by pulling. Tests of near-perfect sheets report strength around 130 GPa and stiffness around 1 TPa. You may hear that graphene is about 200 times stronger than steel. That is a rough comparison that depends on the kind of steel and the test. It does not describe every graphene product. Strength tells you how hard it is to break something. Stiffness tells you how hard it is to stretch it. Electrons can move through graphene in unusual ways. Scientists describe it as having a zero-gap structure and Dirac-like behaviour. It can carry charge and heat very well, but the result depends on the sample, heat level, surface beneath it, and test method. Flaws, grain edges, folds, and dirt can reduce performance. One way to make graphene is exfoliation: peeling layers from graphite. Another is chemical vapor deposition, which grows a film on a surface. Large, clean, even sheets are still hard to make and move. Layers sliding over one another is an issue for stacked layers, not a lone sheet, so real products need real tests, not just claims based on a perfect sample.
groups.low: Graphene is a very thin sheet of carbon. It is just one atom thick, with atoms in a pattern of six-sided shapes, like a honeycomb. Strong bonds hold the atoms in the sheet. Tests of near-perfect sheets show strength around 130 GPa and stiffness around 1 TPa. These are units used to test materials. You may hear that graphene is 200 times stronger than steel. This is a rough claim that depends on the steel and the test. Not every graphene product will be that strong. Strength means how hard it is to break, while stiffness means how hard it is to stretch. Electrons can move through graphene in special ways, described by the terms zero-gap and Dirac-like. Good sheets can carry charge and heat well. But the sheet, its heat level, what it rests on, and the test all matter. Flaws, edges between grains, folds, and dirt can make it work less well. Graphite has many carbon layers, and peeling off a layer is called exfoliation. Another way to make a sheet is chemical vapor deposition, which grows a film on a surface. Making large, clean, even sheets is hard, and moving them is hard too. Layers can slide when stacked, but a single sheet has no other layer to slide against. Test the real product rather than relying on claims about perfect sheets alone.
groups.source_review: Checked original elastic-property study bibliographic abstract and Nobel scientific background. Device-independent mobility and conductivity numbers omitted as not universal.
groups.notes: Qualified steel comparison and corrected monolayer shear-sliding failure explanation.

groups.high: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microbes evolve or acquire mechanisms that reduce a medicine's effectiveness. Bacterial resistance does not mean the patient's body has become resistant. One mechanism involves beta-lactamase enzymes, encoded by resistance genes, which hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring of certain antibiotics. Penicillins and cephalosporins normally inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by targeting penicillin-binding proteins. Breaking the drug's ring can prevent effective binding, allowing bacteria to survive. Different beta-lactamases affect different drugs; clavulanate inhibits some, not all, of these enzymes. Mutations and horizontal transfer of genes, including through plasmids, can spread resistance. Antibiotic exposure selects resistant organisms, while misuse and overuse accelerate selection and transmission. Inadequate sanitation, infection control, diagnostics, and access to appropriate treatment also contribute. The WHO's 2015 Global Action Plan emphasized awareness, surveillance, infection prevention, appropriate antimicrobial use, and sustainable investment. Resistance threatens routine treatment and procedures that depend on infection control. A projection of ten million deaths in 2050 is not a measured death count or a guaranteed outcome. Prescribing should follow clinical evidence, not the assumption that every infection needs an antibiotic. New medicines and diagnostics matter, but preventing infection and preserving existing treatments remain central.
groups.mid: Antimicrobial resistance means germs change or gain ways to survive a medicine. It is the germ, not your body, that becomes resistant. Some bacteria make enzymes called beta-lactamases. These break the beta-lactam ring in certain antibiotics. Penicillins and cephalosporins use that ring to act on penicillin-binding proteins. Those proteins help build the bacterial cell wall. If the drug's ring is broken, it may no longer block the wall being built. The bacteria can survive. Different beta-lactamases act on different drugs. Clavulanate can block some of these enzymes, but not all. Resistance can start with gene changes. Bacteria can also share genes on small DNA pieces called plasmids. An antibiotic may kill the sensitive bacteria while resistant ones remain and spread. Misuse and overuse make this worse. Poor sanitation, weak infection control, lack of tests, and poor access to the right care also matter. WHO's 2015 Global Action Plan called for awareness, tracking resistance, preventing infection, wise use of medicines, and lasting investment. Resistance can make both common infections and medical procedures harder to treat safely. A forecast of ten million deaths in 2050 is not a count of deaths now or a certain future. Use antibiotics on clinical advice, not for every illness. New drugs and tests help. So do clean care and protecting the medicines we already have.
groups.low: Drug resistance happens when germs find ways to survive a medicine; the germs become resistant, not your body. Some bacteria make enzymes called beta-lactamases, small tools made by a cell. These tools can break a part of some drugs called the beta-lactam ring. Penicillins and cephalosporins need this ring to work. They act on penicillin-binding proteins. These help bacteria build their cell walls. Break the drug's ring, and it may fail to stop that work. The bacteria can live on. Not all beta-lactamases attack the same drugs. Clavulanate blocks some of these enzymes, but it does not block all of them. A germ's genes can change. Bacteria can also share genes on small DNA pieces called plasmids. A drug may kill the weaker germs. Resistant germs can stay and spread. Using too many antibiotics, or using them wrongly, makes this worse. Poor sanitation and infection control add to the harm. So do a lack of tests and poor access to the right care. WHO's 2015 Global Action Plan called for public awareness, tracking, infection prevention, wise drug use, and lasting funds. Resistance puts common care and medical procedures at risk. A forecast of ten million deaths in 2050 is not a count of deaths now or a fixed future. Take antibiotics on clinical advice. They are not for every illness. We need new drugs and tests. We also need to prevent infections and protect the drugs we have.
groups.source_review: Checked WHO resistance overview and the named 2015 action-plan framework; avoided presenting older projections as observed facts.
groups.notes: Removed deterministic obsolescence and inevitable sublethal-exposure claims; qualified enzyme inhibition and historical projection.

groups.high: Transit detection measures a star's brightness while an orbiting planet crosses its visible disc. Ignoring limb darkening and blending, the fractional depth is approximately the square of the planet-to-star radius ratio. Earth's radius is about one 109th of the Sun's, giving a depth near 0.0084%, or 84 parts per million: roughly the stated 0.01% scale, not 0.84%. Repeated dips reveal orbital period, and depth helps estimate radius when the star is characterized. A dip alone neither confirms a planet nor establishes habitability. Eclipsing binaries, stellar activity, and instrumental effects can mimic signals, requiring validation and sometimes spectroscopy or radial-velocity follow-up. Transit shapes are not generally sinusoidal. A circumstellar habitable zone describes distances where surface liquid water might be possible under suitable atmospheric conditions; it does not prove water, life, or an Earth-like atmosphere. NASA's Kepler mission operated from 2009 to 2018 and monitored its original field for roughly four years, not a universal 100-day window. TESS, launched in 2018, surveys sectors for about 27 days in its original observing pattern, with longer coverage in overlaps. Kepler's long baseline and TESS's bright nearby targets offer complementary discovery opportunities.
groups.mid: A transit happens when a planet passes across the face of its star. The star looks a little dimmer, and the depth of the dip is roughly the planet-to-star radius ratio squared. This simple rule leaves out effects such as darker edges on a star and light from nearby stars. Earth's radius is about one 109th of the Sun's, so Earth would block about 0.0084% of the Sun's light, or 84 parts per million. That is close to 0.01%, not 0.84%, and repeated dips help show how long an orbit takes. The dip's depth helps estimate size if the star's size is known, but one dip does not prove a planet exists, since two stars eclipsing each other, star activity, or faulty data can look similar. Scientists check the signal and may use spectra or radial-velocity tests; the dip is not usually a smooth sine wave. A habitable zone is a range where liquid surface water might be possible with a suitable atmosphere. It does not prove water or life, and NASA's Kepler mission ran from 2009 to 2018 and watched its first field for about four years, not just 100 days. TESS launched in 2018, and its original plan watched each sector for about 27 days, longer where sectors overlap. Kepler's long view and TESS's bright nearby stars help in different ways.
groups.low: A planet can pass in front of its star, an event called a transit. The star then looks a bit dimmer. The size of the dip helps show the planet's size, using a rough rule that uses the radius of the planet divided by the star's radius, then squares the result. The rule leaves out some effects: a star's edge can be darker, and other stars can add light. Earth's radius is about one 109th of the Sun's, so it would block about 0.0084% of the Sun's light. That is 84 parts per million, close to 0.01%, not 0.84%. Dips that repeat help show the time for one orbit, but to judge planet size, we must know the star's size too. A dip alone does not prove a planet is there, as two stars can eclipse each other. Changes on a star or faults in data can cause dips too. Scientists check these causes and may study the light or the star's small back-and-forth motion. The dip is not usually a smooth sine wave. The habitable zone is where surface water might stay liquid with the right air. It does not prove water or life. NASA's Kepler mission ran from 2009 to 2018 and watched its first patch for about four years, not 100 days. TESS launched in 2018, and its first plan watched each patch for about 27 days. Overlapping patches got longer views. Kepler's long view and TESS's bright nearby stars help find different planets.
groups.source_review: Checked NASA transit explanation, TESS observing sectors, and NASA discussion of the 84-ppm Earth signal. Arithmetic independently checked.
groups.notes: Corrected hundredfold transit-depth error, unsupported habitability confirmation, sinusoidal shape, Kepler baseline, and TESS cadence/sector confusion.

groups.high: A generative large language model predicts a probability distribution over the next token from the preceding context. Tokens may be words, word fragments, or punctuation. GPT-3, described in the 2020 paper Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, is a concrete example with 175 billion parameters and a dense, autoregressive decoder-only Transformer architecture. Causal self-attention combines information from preceding token positions, while positional representations encode order. Training adjusts numerical weights to reduce prediction error across text; generation then selects tokens from the resulting distributions. Larger parameter counts can improve performance alongside adequate data and compute, but do not guarantee truth, reasoning quality, or a particular embedding dimension. The original GPT-3 was not a mixture-of-experts model and did not use every positional technique developed later. Few-shot prompting supplies examples in the context without updating model weights. Supervised fine-tuning and human-feedback training are separate adaptation stages used in some systems, not inherent requirements of every language model. Standard attention has quadratic sequence-length costs, although implementations and alternative architectures differ. Models can produce plausible false statements and reflect training-data biases. External retrieval can add documents, but next-token prediction alone does not verify claims against a trusted database. Useful deployment therefore requires evaluation, appropriate sources, and safeguards.
groups.mid: A large language model predicts the next token from the text before it. A token may be a word, part of a word, or a mark like a comma. GPT-3 is one example. The 2020 paper Language Models are Few-Shot Learners describes its 175 billion parameters. These are learned number values, or weights. GPT-3 uses a dense, decoder-only Transformer. Its self-attention system uses earlier tokens to help predict the next one. Position information shows their order. Training changes the weights to reduce prediction errors. When it writes, the model picks tokens from the chances it has calculated. More weights, good data, and enough computing power can help. Size alone does not guarantee true answers or good reasoning. It does not fix the size of every internal text representation. The original GPT-3 was not a mixture-of-experts model. It did not use all newer ways to mark positions. Few-shot prompting puts examples in the prompt; it does not change model weights. Fine-tuning and learning from human feedback are separate steps used in some systems. Standard attention can become much more costly as text grows, though designs and software differ. A model may write false claims that sound convincing. It can also repeat bias in its training text. Adding document search can help supply sources, but prediction alone does not check truth. Testing, suitable sources, and safeguards still matter.
groups.low: A large language model predicts the next token in a piece of text. A token can be a word, part of a word, or a comma, and GPT-3 is one such model. A 2020 paper, Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, describes it. It has 175 billion learned number values, called parameters or weights. It uses a dense, decoder-only Transformer. A tool called self-attention helps it use the tokens that came before. Position information tells it their order. During training, the model changes its weights to make fewer errors. When it writes, it works out the chances of each next token. It then picks one and goes on. More weights can help if there is enough good data and computing power. Size does not make every answer true. It does not promise sound reasoning or a fixed size for each inner text map. The first GPT-3 was not a mixture-of-experts model. It did not use all newer ways to mark word order. Few-shot prompting means adding examples to the prompt without changing the weights. Fine-tuning and learning from human feedback are other steps. Not all models use them. Standard attention can cost much more as text gets longer. Other designs can differ. The model can make up facts and repeat bias. A search tool can bring in documents. But predicting text is not the same as checking facts. Tests, good sources, and safeguards are still needed.
groups.source_review: Checked original GPT-3 paper, using 175B as a specific historical example rather than a universal/current LLM specification.
groups.notes: Corrected unsupported architecture, MoE, positional-method, embedding-dimension, and guaranteed emergent-ability claims.
